title: Demand signals can unlock small-firm digital market participation more reliably than training alone
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11460, Barriers to Market Access: Experimental Tests of Supply- and Demand-Side Strategies
geography: Small enterprises in Georgia participating in randomized training and demand-incentive experiments, with surveys conducted between 2018 and 2025

training_effect.value: supply-side training did not increase digital participation

initial_interest.value: the null participation effect occurred despite high initial interest in the training intervention

barrier_interpretation.value: the result is consistent with barriers beyond simple awareness or skill provision

observations.method: Randomized experiment comparing a supply-side training intervention with control firms; data and code are documented in the World Bank reproducibility package.
observations.uncertainty: The result is specific to the training design, participating Georgian enterprises, digital-market context, and study period; it does not show that all training is ineffective or that skills never matter.
observations.subgroup: Small firms with different baseline digital readiness, organizational capacity, confidence, products, networks, and ability to absorb a new sales channel.
observations.counterinterpretation: Training quality, timing, content, or implementation may have been insufficient; a different curriculum or paired demand might produce different results.

market_access_effect.unit: percentage-point increase in market access from a conditional purchase order

larger_payment.value: a payment six times larger produced only a modest additional increase

complementarity.value: the study found no complementarity between training and demand incentives

mechanism.value: a credible buyer and first transaction can lower behavioral and organizational barriers to digital-market entry

observations.method: Randomized demand-side experiment using conditional purchase orders and payment-intensity variation among Georgian small enterprises.
observations.uncertainty: The effect concerns the study's market-access measure and treatment design; it does not establish durable revenue, profitability, employment, productivity, or consumer-welfare effects.
observations.subgroup: Small firms with different readiness for e-commerce, products, administrative capacity, and ability to fulfill a conditional order; buyers and intermediaries also shape the treatment environment.
observations.counterinterpretation: A purchase order may operate as temporary subsidy, validation, or working-capital relief rather than a pure demand signal; larger payments may have weak marginal effects because the main constraint is not cash alone.

denominator.unit: Georgia small-enterprise follow-up comparison after demand shock

persistence.value: the treatment effects largely dissipated as control firms caught up

readiness_selection.value: firms with higher baseline e-commerce readiness remained more likely to engage in digital markets several years later

acceleration.value: there is suggestive evidence that the demand shock accelerated adoption among higher-readiness firms

growth_barrier.value: remaining barriers appear more behavioral and organizational than simple skill or capital deficits

observations.method: Follow-up surveys and longer-run comparison of firms exposed to the randomized interventions, with the paper's reproducibility package documenting the analysis workflow.
observations.uncertainty: The longer-run pattern is not a universal adoption forecast; persistence varies with readiness, market conditions, treatment intensity, firm survival, and later access to buyers or platforms.
observations.subgroup: Digitally ready and less-ready small firms, firms that survive and remain observable, platform participants, buyers, and local business ecosystems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Control firms catching up may reflect diffusion or broader market change rather than a failure of demand incentives; persistent readiness differences may partly reflect unmeasured firm quality.

boundary: This record adds a causal demand-signal-to-digital-market-participation route for small enterprises, with null training, conditional purchase-order, payment-intensity, longer-run catch-up, and baseline-readiness evidence. It does not establish durable profits, employment, productivity, firm survival, broad consumer welfare, universal training failure, or generalization beyond the Georgian experiments.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank working-paper PDF and reproducibility package were reviewed for the randomized training and demand experiments, 26-percentage-point purchase-order effect, payment-intensity comparison, no training-demand complementarity, follow-up persistence, baseline readiness, and behavioral/organizational barrier interpretation.
